parts:
Dear Eric,

I just came to know from one colleague that DISTANCE doesn't work in
mountain topography. I am really frustrated at this last minute. But,
according to Marques and Buckland (2004), Marques et al. (2007), Strindberg,
Buckland and Thomas (2004), I am still believe that good survey design (with
automated survey design engine) and inclusion of covariates might work to
estimate group density of Assamese macaque in mountain topography of Nepal.
Could you please suggest me as early as possible? I am worrying too much
that if it doesn't work, I have to leave this project which is really
frustrating!

Sincerely,
Ganga

messages.subject: Re: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
parts:
Hi Ganga=2CThere is nothing preventing you from designing a good survey for=
any geographic area. =20
In this paper by Len Thomas=2C we had a geographically complex study area. =
We couldn't afford to sample every fjord=2C so we divided the area up into=
32 manageable-sized pieces in GIS=2C and randomly sampled 5 of them. We u=
sed Distance to design good=2C design-unbiased surveys for each of those ar=
eas. The design is described here:
http://www.marinemammal.org/mmru/williams/thomas%20williams%20sandilands%20=
jcrm%20survey%20design%202007.pdf
and the analysis of the resulting survey data is described here:http://www.=
marinemammal.org/mmru/williams/williams%20thomas%20jcrm%202007%20015-028.pd=
f
You'd have to "flatten" your 3D study area in GIS into some 2D shapefiles=
=2C but the automated survey design algorithms in Distance work fine in com=
plex areas. The amount of survey effort you can conduct is a function of l=
ogistics and funding=3B not of the algorithms that Distance can handle. I =
don't know what you mean by the use of covariates=2C but it sounds like you=
have some issues you need to work out at the design stage (e.g.=2C having =
a steep versus a flat stratum=2C or bare rock/vegetation stratum). It's go=
od to sort these out at the design stage=2C rather than relying on unnecess=
arily complex analyses later on. =20
Good luck=2CRob

messages.subject: Re: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
parts:
The only reason why mountain topography causes problems is that it can
be impossible to traverse randomly-positioned lines, so that a random
design may need to be compromised to some degree. It is better to work
with flat projections of all distances and areas. So line length is the
length of the line on a 2D map, distances of detected animals from the
line are horizontal distances, and the size of the study area is its
area on a 2D map.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
parts:
If it is difficult to traverse random lines, then a point transect
option can work well in many circumstances, e.g. birds that typically do
not show much reaction to the observer. If you rely on flushing animals
to detect them, then point transect sampling will not work, as you are
likely to flush those near the point before reaching it.

Typically, you can expect lower precision for the same effort when you
use point transects instead of line transects, so usually, the option
would only be used where it is impractical to use line transect
sampling, or where it is believed that the assumptions are easier to
satisfy when surveying from points rather than lines.

Steve Buckland
